Not the point. AI taking jobs is not (at least not now) a phenomenon that has to do with the nature of "job" or the capabilites of AI. It is to do with ppl like you who are "AI forward", whatever that really means. The idea that AI = productivity gains MUST, in the eyes of a capatalist, lead to a reduction of staff costs. Simple as that. Moving beyond that, the fact that the NUMBER of jobs increased has no correlation to the question "will my job be taken?" As mentioned in the video, tellers' work content evolved and had to provide more than just handing out cash to ppl. That would require a shift in competencies. The old skills tend to be more basic and therefore old staff will have a harder time adjusting and may get phased out. The one thing that really is worth discussing is not "will AI take my job?" It is "how / how well will the world operate once AI becomes the driving force of productivity?" There are arguments for and against the idea that "this is just another human invention that increases productivity, and we've survived all the previous such advancements so far". There are studies pointing to quality issues, security problems, short term gains vs long term deterioration, AI psychosis, adverse mental health etc etc. Naming a fear-based topic in order to further peddle the urgency for an AI takeover is not a fair approach

The big tech only perspectives kind of get tiring after a while and make me realize how much of a bubble these workers actually reside in. Not everyone who works as a developer works in big tech, or has a desire to work in big tech. In fact, I would say THE VAST MAJORITY of developers do not work in big tech. Literally every industry (and probably every company) has a need for developers/technical workers. Instead of whining about how tough things are and quitting the industry entirely because 5 companies treat their employees like numbers, try one of the other thousands of mid to small size companies in pretty much any industry you find interesting. I think people who do this would discover that: 1. You are likely more valued when the company isn't a large tech company, and your immediate team is smaller 2. You have more to offer in helping that particular company grow 3. Benefits (and pay) can be just as good in smaller more established companies 4. More control over the projects you work on and less stress in general 5. You have higher flexibility in how you choose to work 6. A lot more leverage in terms of what you want because they desperately will not want you to leave if you are the go-to person. They aren't going to replace the only person who knows anything about development with AI. Find a small to medium size family-oriented company (not a chaotic start-up), make an immediate impact, be treated like a person rather than a number, pursue your passions and hobbies and all the other crap with the time and sanity you've gained back.
